items.title: NTU Pair
body: NTU Pair is an innovative matchmaking platform I developed to foster meaningful connections among NTU students. Instead of relying on traditional swipe mechanisms, the platform utilizes psychological assessments to evaluate interpersonal compatibility. By leveraging custom matching algorithms, the system pairs users with compatible profiles to encourage deeper, more meaningful interactions.

Following its launch, the web application quickly attracted over 1,600 verified student users. However, encountering early security challenges including cross-site scripting (XSS), denial of service (DoS) attempts, and credential stuffing, it spurred me to deepen my expertise in cybersecurity and re-architect the system using secure coding standards. This hands-on experience in rapid incident response and defensive engineering directly informs how I build more resilient full-stack applications today.

items.title: Whiskers IDE
supporting: A Web-Based IDE for Writing Scratch-Like Code
body: Learning to code wasn't easy for me. I spent years mastering Scratch, yet struggled when transitioning to JavaScript because of complex syntax. I created Whiskers to ensure the next generation doesn't have to face that same brick wall.

Whiskers is the ultimate stepping stone for young learners transitioning from block-based coding to text-based programming. While drag-and-drop platforms like Scratch teach brilliant logical thinking, switching to traditional languages like JavaScript can feel overwhelming. Whiskers bridges this gap by using familiar Scratch concepts expressed through a simple, text-based syntax that seamlessly aligns with JavaScript logic.

With a full-featured Monaco Editor (drop-in blocks, autocomplete, and syntax highlighting), multi-sprite support, and instant browser preview, kids can naturally evolve from dragging code blocks to writing real, professional code with confidence.

items.title: LifeOS Automation System
body: LifeOS Automation System is a Python service designed to bridge a team's Notion workspace with a MongoDB database, allowing project groups to manage their workflows entirely inside Notion while a robust backend engine handles consistency, conflict resolution, and planning algorithms behind the scenes. Built with a 7-person team, the system solves the fundamental challenges of using human-centric tools for automated operations, such as concurrent edits, missing built-in versioning, and complex multi-page schedule mirroring.

As the designer and implementer of the core synchronization algorithm, I engineered a version-state model that tracks pages across four distinct states: UP_TO_DATE, AHEAD, BEHIND, and NOT_TRACKED. By comparing Notion's last-edited timestamps against persisted database versions to eliminate ad-hoc diffing. To handle complex project topologies where a single schedule must map to multiple individual user pages, I developed a canonical document mapping architecture with fan-out linking and automated collaborator diffing. Combined with an asynchronous convergent sync loop that handles bounded re-sweeps, the system now reliably synchronizes live team workspaces, automatically provisions new collaborators, and recovers from out-of-order updates without manual copy-pasting.

items.title: Virtual Makerspace
supporting: An Online Replica of The NTUEE Makerspace
body: In my first year as a student association member, my life revolved around the NTUEE Makerspace, which is a paradise for those who love to create things from scratch. However, the Makerspace was often messy due to the lack of proper organization and management. Hence, I came up with the idea of creating an online replica of the makerspace, combining the current borrowing form, the 3D printing reservation form, the "all tools and ICs" Excel page, and a brand new virtual 3D model of the Makerspace that behaves as Google street view. All the systems combine into one big metaverse, where students can check online if an object is present in the Makerspace, find where it is on the website, and borrow it immediately.

From the NTU Pair experience, I knew that I needed more people to accomplish this grand construction; thus, I formed a team of 25 to kickstart the project in May 2023. Since the team members were almost new to web programming, I wrote teaching material and held physical programming classes for my team members to learn.

This was my first time leading a big team with two levels of direct reports. To organize this complicated structure, I learned project management through online courses and implemented them to standardize our workflows.

After three months, we created a prototype of the website with some basic functions. Shortly after, the project was handed over to the information department of the NTUEE student association for annual maintenance, which signals the end of my journey as the visionary of NTUEE Virtual Makerspace.

items.title: Urban Radius
supporting: A Simulation of an Algorithm to Define a City's Borders.
body: Can we measure a city's "true size" without relying on arbitrary administrative borders?

When we compare cities, we often run into the "boundary problem." A city with vast, sparse suburbs can appear larger than a dense, polycentric metropolis simply because of how its administrative lines were drawn decades ago.

Inspired by Ray Delahanty's video on YouTube, "Can We Agree On the 4 Major U.S. Cities?", I started thinking about how we might standardize this. How do we move beyond lines on a map to capture the "true" functional footprint of a city?

Derived from the academic H-Index, I came up with the idea of the Urban Radius and built a prototype implementing it, along with an interactive website to experiment with different parameters and see how the calculated boundaries change. The mathematical description and the algorithm is explained in my live simulation website.

items.title: Robotic Chameleon — Cockroach Catcher
supporting: First Place, Silicon Motion Corporate Award

images.alt: Presenting on stage for the final round

body: For the 2025 MakeNTU Competition, our team built a robotic chameleon capable of tracking and catching cockroaches using computer vision and a Raspberry Pi. Within 24 hours, we completed the project from the first line of code to the final presentation.

The system utilized a phone camera to capture consecutive images of the environment, which were then processed my a computer vision algorithm to identify cockroaches based on their shape and color. Once a cockroach was detected, the phone would send the coordinates on the image to the Raspberry Pi, which would then warp those coordinates into real-world positions using perspective transformation and feed the positions into a PID controller algorithm to determine the movement of the chameleon. The chameleon was equipped with a mechanical tongue made from a servo motor, which could rapidly fire to catch the cockroach once it was within range.

A significant breakthrough I contributed to was designing a reverse proxy to enable the communications between the phone's camera and the backend image recognition algorithm on the Raspberry Pi, which was otherwise blocked due to HTTP security reasons. In the end, we successfully made it to the final round on stage. Our efforts were recognized by the judging panel sponsored by Silicon Motion, awarding us first place in the corporate award category.

items.title: HelpMet — An AR Navigation Assistant for Motorcyclists

images.alt: Presenting on stage for the final round

body: For the 2024 MakeNTU competition, we created an AR navigation assistant mounted inside a motorcycle helmet, using speech recognition and projection technologies to help riders navigate through the city. Our aim was to eliminate traffic accidents caused by phone distraction, and help motorcyclists "leave home happily and return safely."

Our prototype used a Raspberry Pi as the main controller, connected to a microphone for voice input, an OLED display for AR output, and an online website to simulate motorcycle movement around the city and location tracking (because it is hard to demonstrate moving around during demo time). The system can recognize voice commands to set destinations and provide turn-by-turn navigation instructions given by the Google Maps API. The instructions would then be displayed on the OLED screen inside the helmet, using the reflection of the helmet visor to create an AR effect.

My role in this project was the system architect. Since the APIs voice recognition modules, and input commands were all asynchronous by nature, I designed a multi-threaded architecture to handle different tasks simultaneously. This architecture idea was brought from hardware flip-flop designs, where check bits and clock signals are used to synchronize different modules. By implementing this architecture, our system was able to respond to user commands in real-time, providing a smooth and efficient navigation experience.

items.title: Online Medical Diagnosis and Simulation Systems

images.alt: Our team at the CTCI headquarters office
Our team in front of the competition poster
Demonstration of the Online Diagnosis Process

links.label: Our project on the Ministry of Education website

body: In the summer of 2023, I joined SLEKMED, an educational startup composed of 60 medical students, tailored to help high school students explore and understand medical-related academic studies. Serving as one of the two product developers with a tech background, I collaborated with medical students to create web-based diagnosis simulation systems as teaching aids. During my time at SLEKMED, I worked on two major projects: the Hyponatremia Diagnosis Simulation System and the Online-Hospital AI Simulation system.

**The Hyponatremia system** allowed students to practice diagnosing and treating hyponatremia cases through an interactive web interface. Collaborating with medical students, we designed the algorithm to simulate real-life scenarios, including patient history, symptoms, and lab results. Students could make decisions on diagnosis and treatment, receiving immediate feedback on their choices. Our system was awarded funding from the Ministry of Education's *Start-up Simulation Platform for University and Tertiary College* program, recognizing its potential to enhance medical education.

**The Online-Hospital AI Simulation System** was a different approach to medical education. This system used Notion and Gather as the user interface, allowing students to navigate a virtual hospital environment and use Notion's databases to simulate writing medical records, ordering tests, and prescribing treatments. To simulate patient interactions, we integrated an AI chatbot, enabling dynamic conversations with virtual patients. This project won the first place in the *2024 CTCI AI Competiton* with a grand award of 400K NTD, standing out among 40+ teams nationwide.

items.title: Acquired Universe
supporting: A Space-Time Display of Companies Covered on the Acquired Podcast
body: I've been listening to the *Acquired Podcast* for two years, and the relationships between the companies inspired me to create this graphical interface of space, time, and connection for the listeners of the podcast.

The *Acquired Universe* includes three main views. First, the time-elapse view demonstrates the appearance of company stories in the chronological order of *Acquired* episodes. Second, the graph view displays the connections between companies, sourced from *Acquired's* episode captions. Third, the timeline view allows the user to view the major events of each company mapped on a single timeline.

items.title: Light Bike
supporting: An LED show mounted on a bicycle

links.label: A short demo video of my project (YouTube)

body: I built a programmable LED light show for a bicycle using LED strips, a multiplexer, and a D1 Mini microcontroller. All the programming, soldering and wiring are customized for my bike and made from scratch, and system can be remotely controlled via a web-app, allowing dynamic lighting effects while riding.

items.title: NTUEE Light Dance Props
body: NTUEE Light Dance is an annual performance organized by the NTUEE Student Association, where students showcase their creativity through synchronized light shows. In 2023, I contributed to the event by designing and building LED props for the performers. Our theme that year was *Bartender*, and my team and I created three LED bar cupboards that can be transformed into an arsenal during the performance. We also created a bar counter that can be split in half during the show. These props served as the main stage decorations, enhancing the visual impact of the performance.

items.title: NTU Food
supporting: A random food selection website for NTU students
body: I built a web-app using *vanilla* JavaScript to help NTU students randomly select food options on campus. The web-app was featured in a famous Taiwanese YouTuber *Joeman*'s video reviewing NTU food options and has on average 100 users online a day.
